goals: Explain why a country needs a parliament and why India has two Houses

slides.heading: Parliament: The Two Houses
slides.body_md: Part 1: why we need a **parliament**, the **Rajya Sabha**, the **Lok Sabha** and their **powers**.

visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: A country with millions of people cannot make every law by a vote of all citizens. It needs a body that speaks for them. In this part we study the Parliament of India, why it has two Houses, how each House is chosen, and what powers each one holds.

slides.heading: Why do we need a parliament?

rows: Debating and passing bills so that they become laws
Speaking for the people and for the States
Questioning ministers and being able to remove the government
A forum where public issues are discussed openly

visual.alt: Table of the four functions of Parliament: law-making; representation of the people and the States; control of the executive by questioning ministers and being able to remove the government; and debate on public issues

slides.narration: A parliament has four main tasks. It makes laws. It represents the people and the States. It controls the executive by questioning ministers and by being able to remove a government that loses support. And it is a forum for open debate on public issues. All four tasks matter in a democracy.

slides.heading: Why two Houses?

rows: One House for the people, one for the States
A bill is studied twice, which checks hasty decisions
The States are heard in making laws for the Union
Most States have one House; six have Legislative Councils (as of 2024)

visual.alt: Table of reasons for two Houses: two kinds of representation, reconsideration of bills, federal balance, and in the States most have one House while six have a Legislative Council as of 2024

slides.narration: Many federal countries have two Houses. One House speaks for the people and the other for the units of the federation. A second House also lets every bill be studied twice, which checks hasty decisions. Most States of India have one House, and only six have a Legislative Council, as of two thousand twenty four.

visual.alt: Comparison chart of the two Houses of Parliament. The Rajya Sabha represents the States, has at most 250 members of whom 238 are elected and 12 nominated by the President, is chosen indirectly by State Assembly members by single transferable vote, has a six year term with one third retiring every second year, a minimum age of 30, and special powers under Article 249 and Article 312. The Lok Sabha represents the people, allows up to 550 elected members with 543 constituencies as of 2024, is chosen directly by first past the post, has a five year term unless dissolved earlier, a minimum age of 25, and special powers over money bills and no-confidence motions
visual.caption: The two Houses compared.

slides.narration: This chart compares the two Houses. The Rajya Sabha represents the States, has at most two hundred fifty members, and is chosen indirectly. The Lok Sabha represents the people and is chosen directly. The Rajya Sabha members serve six years and one third retire every second year. The Lok Sabha serves five years unless it is dissolved earlier.

slides.heading: The Rajya Sabha: composition and election

rows: For art, literature, science and social service
Elected members of State Assemblies; single transferable vote

visual.alt: Table about the Rajya Sabha: it represents the States; at most 250 members, 238 elected and 12 nominated for art, literature, science and social service; elected by the elected members of State Assemblies by the single transferable vote; six year term; a permanent House

slides.narration: The Rajya Sabha represents the States. It has at most two hundred fifty members, of whom two hundred thirty eight are elected and twelve are nominated by the President for distinction in art, literature, science and social service. The elected members are chosen by the elected members of the State Legislative Assemblies, by the single transferable vote.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: who votes for Dr Mehra?
slides.body_md: A Rajya Sabha seat from the imagined State of Palmora falls vacant. Trace how it is filled.

headers: Step in the imagined case of Dr Mehra
rows: A Rajya Sabha seat from the imagined State of Palmora falls vacant
Several candidates are put up for the seat
Only the elected members of the Palmora Legislative Assembly vote
They vote by single transferable vote, in order of preference
The candidate with the quota of votes is declared elected

visual.alt: Worked example table of an imagined Rajya Sabha election from Palmora: a seat falls vacant, candidates are put up, only the elected members of the State Legislative Assembly vote, by single transferable vote in order of preference, and the candidate with the quota is elected
visual.caption: The voters are Assembly members, not the public.

slides.narration: Imagine that a Rajya Sabha seat from the State of Palmora falls vacant. Several candidates stand. The voters are not the public but only the elected members of the Palmora Legislative Assembly. They vote in order of preference, by the single transferable vote, and the candidate who reaches the quota of votes is declared elected.

slides.heading: A permanent House

rows: About one-third of the House retires and new members join

visual.alt: Table of an imagined cycle of retirement: members elected in 2026 retire in 2032, those elected in 2028 retire in 2034, those elected in 2030 retire in 2036; in every two years about one-third of the House retires and new members join
visual.caption: Members stagger, so the House never dissolves.

slides.narration: The Rajya Sabha is called a permanent House. It is never dissolved as a whole. Members serve six years, and about one third of them retire every second year. In this imagined cycle the batch elected in two thousand twenty six retires in two thousand thirty two. New members join as others retire, so the House always has sitting members.

slides.heading: Unequal representation

rows: Allotted broadly by population, so unequal

visual.alt: Table comparing second chambers: the United States Senate gives two seats to every State; the Rajya Sabha allots seats broadly by population so it is unequal; imagined Rhenia gives three seats to every province
visual.caption: India differs from an equal-seat second chamber.

slides.narration: Seats in the Rajya Sabha are allotted to the States broadly by population, so larger States have more seats. This differs from the Senate of the United States, where every State has two seats. It also differs from the imagined Rhenia, where every province has three. Some argue that equal seats protect small units, while others argue that population should count.

slides.heading: The Lok Sabha: composition and term

rows: Directly elected by first past the post
Up to 550 elected allowed; 543 constituencies (as of 2024)
Two Anglo-Indian seats ended by the 104th Amendment (2019, in effect 2020)

visual.alt: Table about the Lok Sabha: it represents the people; directly elected by first past the post; the Constitution allows up to 550 elected members with 543 constituencies as of 2024; the two nominated Anglo-Indian seats ended with the 104th Amendment passed in 2019 and in effect from 2020; five year term unless dissolved earlier

slides.narration: The Lok Sabha is directly elected by first past the post. As of two thousand twenty four, the Constitution allows up to five hundred fifty elected members, and there are five hundred forty three constituencies. The nomination of two Anglo-Indian members ended with the one hundred fourth Amendment, passed in two thousand nineteen. The term is five years, unless the House is dissolved earlier.

slides.body_md: The Lok Sabha is dissolved in the third year. What happens to the Rajya Sabha?
slides.narration: Recall which House can be dissolved.

slides.heading: Powers shared by both Houses

rows: A bill must pass both Houses
Both Houses pass them by a special majority
Elected members of both Houses vote
All members of both Houses vote

visual.alt: Table of the powers shared by both Houses: passing ordinary bills, passing constitutional amendments by a special majority, and taking part in the election of the President by elected members and of the Vice-President by all members

slides.narration: Both Houses have equal powers in many matters. A bill must pass both Houses to become an ordinary law. Constitutional amendments must pass both by a special majority. The elected members of both Houses take part in electing the President, and all members of both Houses vote for the Vice-President.

visual.caption: Path of a money bill.

slides.narration: A money bill deals with taxes, borrowing and spending. It can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha, and the Speaker certifies whether a bill is a money bill. After the Lok Sabha passes it, the Rajya Sabha has only fourteen days. It may return the bill with suggestions, but the Lok Sabha may accept or reject them. If the Rajya Sabha does nothing, the bill is deemed passed.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a money bill in practice
slides.body_md: Follow the imagined Coastal Levy Bill, a tax on dried fish exports, through the two Houses.
bullets: The Lok Sabha **decides** a money bill
The Rajya Sabha can only **delay** it

rows: The Speaker certifies it as a money bill; the Lok Sabha passes it
It is sent to the Rajya Sabha, which debates it
The Rajya Sabha returns it with two suggestions
The Lok Sabha rejects both suggestions
The bill goes on in the form the Lok Sabha passed it

visual.alt: Worked example table of the imagined Coastal Levy Bill: on day one the Speaker certifies it as a money bill and the Lok Sabha passes it; on day two it goes to the Rajya Sabha; on day eight the Rajya Sabha returns it with two suggestions; on day nine the Lok Sabha rejects them; the bill goes on in the form the Lok Sabha passed it
visual.caption: A money bill is settled by the Lok Sabha.

slides.narration: Take the imagined Coastal Levy Bill. The Speaker certifies it as a money bill, and the Lok Sabha passes it. The Rajya Sabha debates it and returns it with two suggestions. The Lok Sabha rejects both. The bill then goes on in the form the Lok Sabha passed, since on a money bill the Lok Sabha has the last word.

headers: Special power of the Rajya Sabha
rows: A two-thirds resolution lets Parliament make a law on a State List subject in the national interest
A two-thirds resolution lets Parliament create a new All India Service

visual.alt: Table of the special powers of the Rajya Sabha: under Article 249 a two-thirds resolution lets Parliament make a law on a State List subject in the national interest; under Article 312 a two-thirds resolution lets Parliament create a new All India Service; the Rajya Sabha has these because it represents the States

slides.narration: The Rajya Sabha has special powers because it represents the States. Under Article two forty nine, if two thirds of the members present and voting pass a resolution in the national interest, Parliament may make a law on a State List subject. Under Article three twelve, a similar resolution lets Parliament create a new All India Service.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: At most 250 (238 + 12); six years; one-third retire every two years
Direct election; up to 550 allowed, 543 seats; five years
Lok Sabha: money bills, no confidence. Rajya Sabha: Articles 249 and 312

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: functions of Parliament, why two Houses, the Rajya Sabha, the Lok Sabha and the special powers of each House

slides.narration: To sum up. Parliament makes laws, represents, controls the executive and debates. India has two Houses so that both the people and the States are heard. The Rajya Sabha has at most two hundred fifty members and serves six years. The Lok Sabha is directly elected for five years. The Lok Sabha leads on money bills and no confidence, while the Rajya Sabha has special powers under two Articles.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Say **indirectly elected** for the Rajya Sabha
Give **238 + 12** for the Rajya Sabha and **543** for the Lok Sabha, with the date
Remember **14 days** for a money bill
Support each point with an example

rows: The Rajya Sabha is elected by voters
Elected indirectly by the elected members of State Assemblies
The Rajya Sabha can reject a money bill
It can only delay it for 14 days
Both Houses can remove the Council of Ministers
Only the Lok Sabha can pass a no-confidence motion

visual.alt: Table of common mistakes in Part 1 and what to write instead

slides.narration: A few tips. Say that the Rajya Sabha is indirectly elected. Give the numbers with the date as of two thousand twenty four. Remember fourteen days for a money bill. Remember that only the Lok Sabha can pass a no confidence motion. And in longer answers, support each point with a short example.

slides.narration: A law begins as a bill, and a government that makes laws must also answer for how it works. In this part we follow a bill through Parliament, look at the tools by which Parliament holds the executive to account, and see how Parliament keeps its own house in order.

slides.heading: Kinds of bills

rows: Introduced by a minister; carries government policy
Introduced by a member who is not a minister; rarely passed
Can start in either House; both Houses must pass it
Taxes, borrowing and spending; starts only in the Lok Sabha

visual.alt: Table of kinds of bills: government bills introduced by a minister; private member bills introduced by a member who is not a minister; ordinary bills that can start in either House; and money bills under Article 110 about taxes, borrowing and spending that start only in the Lok Sabha

slides.narration: A government bill is brought by a minister and carries the policy of the government. A private member bill is brought by a member who is not a minister, and is rarely passed. An ordinary bill may start in either House. A money bill, under Article one ten, concerns taxes, borrowing and spending and starts only in the Lok Sabha.

slides.narration: This flowchart shows the path of an ordinary bill. It is introduced, debated and voted on in the first House. Then the same stages are repeated in the other House. After both Houses pass it, the President gives assent, and the bill becomes an Act. If the Houses disagree, a joint sitting may be called.

slides.heading: The readings in detail

rows: The bill is introduced and its aim stated; no detailed debate
The principles and clauses are debated; a committee may study it
The final vote on the bill as a whole

visual.alt: Table of the readings of a bill: first reading to introduce it, second reading to debate its principles and clauses with a possible committee reference, consideration clause by clause, and third reading for the final vote

slides.narration: At the first reading the bill is introduced and its aim is stated. At the second reading the principles and the clauses are debated, and the House may send the bill to a committee. Then the clauses are taken one by one, and amendments are considered. At the third reading the House takes the final vote on the whole bill.

Give assent; it cannot be sent back for reconsideration
No time limit is set, which gave rise to the pocket veto

visual.alt: Table of the options of the President on a bill: an ordinary bill may be assented to or returned once and if passed again assent must follow; a money bill cannot be returned; no time limit is set, giving rise to the pocket veto

slides.narration: After both Houses pass a bill, it goes to the President. On an ordinary bill the President may give assent, or return it once for reconsideration. If Parliament passes it again, the President must give assent. A money bill cannot be returned. Because no time limit is set, delay in assent has been called the pocket veto.

slides.heading: The joint sitting

nodes.label: An ordinary bill passes one House
The other House rejects it, disagrees on changes, or delays it
A joint sitting is called (Article 108)
The Speaker presides; a majority of those present and voting decides

visual.alt: Flow of a joint sitting: an ordinary bill passes one House; the other House rejects it, disagrees on changes or delays it for over six months; a joint sitting is called under Article 108; the Speaker presides and a majority of those present and voting decides
visual.caption: The joint sitting

slides.narration: If the two Houses cannot agree on an ordinary bill, a joint sitting may be called under Article one oh eight. This can happen if one House rejects the bill, if they disagree on changes, or if more than six months pass without the other House acting. The Speaker presides, and a majority of members present and voting decides. Since the Lok Sabha is larger, its view is likely to prevail.

slides.narration: In a parliamentary system the government must answer to the legislature. This chart shows the main tools. Members debate and question ministers, approve or refuse bills, vote on the budget, examine spending through the Public Accounts Committee, study the work of ministries in committees, and the Lok Sabha can pass a motion of no confidence.

rows: The first hour of a sitting; members question ministers
A practice, not in the rules as such: urgent matters raised without notice
A member draws a minister's attention to a matter of urgent public importance
Sets aside the day's business to discuss an urgent public matter (Lok Sabha)

slides.narration: Question Hour is the first hour of a sitting, in which members question ministers. Zero Hour follows it. It is a practice and is not in the rules as such, and members use it to raise urgent matters without notice. Calling attention draws a minister to a matter of urgent public importance. An adjournment motion, in the Lok Sabha, sets aside the day business to discuss such a matter.

nodes.label: The budget is presented in the Lok Sabha
The Lok Sabha debates and votes on the demands for grants
Money is spent as Parliament allowed
The Comptroller and Auditor General audits the accounts
The Public Accounts Committee examines the reports

visual.caption: Financial control

slides.narration: The executive cannot spend money without the approval of Parliament. The budget is presented in the Lok Sabha, which debates and votes on the demands for grants. The Rajya Sabha may discuss the budget but does not vote on the grants. Afterwards the Comptroller and Auditor General audits the accounts, and the Public Accounts Committee examines the reports.

slides.heading: Parliamentary committees

rows: Permanent; for example the Public Accounts Committee
Begun in 1993; follow groups of ministries and their budgets
Ad hoc; members of both Houses; formed for a particular bill or matter

visual.alt: Table of the kinds of parliamentary committee: standing committees that are permanent such as the Public Accounts Committee; department-related standing committees begun in 1993 that follow groups of ministries; and ad hoc joint parliamentary committees of both Houses for a particular bill or matter

slides.narration: Parliament works through committees. Standing committees are permanent, and include the Public Accounts Committee. The department related standing committees, begun in nineteen ninety three, follow groups of ministries and their budgets. Joint parliamentary committees are ad hoc. They have members of both Houses and are formed for a particular bill or matter.

slides.heading: Why committees matter

rows: A small group can study clauses that the full House has no time for
They can hear experts and groups affected by a bill
Members of different parties often work together there
They scrutinise the executive through the year

visual.alt: Table of why committees matter: detailed study, hearing experts, cooperation among members of different parties, and scrutiny of the executive through the year

slides.narration: The full House has little time, and so committees matter. A small group can study the clauses of a bill in detail. It can hear experts and groups who are affected. Members of different parties often cooperate there. And committees scrutinise the executive through the year, and not only when the House is sitting.

slides.heading: Parliament regulating itself

rows: Presides over the Lok Sabha; keeps order and discipline; certifies money bills
The Vice-President presides over the Rajya Sabha and keeps order
Also decides cases of disqualification for defection

visual.alt: Table of how Parliament regulates itself: the Speaker presides over the Lok Sabha, keeps order and certifies money bills; the Chairman, who is the Vice-President, presides over the Rajya Sabha; the presiding officer also decides cases of disqualification for defection

slides.narration: Parliament also keeps order in its own work. The Speaker presides over the Lok Sabha, keeps order and discipline, and certifies money bills. The Vice-President is the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha and keeps order there. The presiding officer also decides cases of disqualification under the anti defection law.

slides.heading: The anti-defection law

nodes.label: 1985: the 52nd Amendment adds the Tenth Schedule
A member who leaves the party or disobeys the whip may be disqualified
The presiding officer decides
2003: the 91st Amendment removes the split exception

visual.alt: Flow of the anti-defection law: in 1985 the 52nd Amendment adds the Tenth Schedule; a member who leaves the party or disobeys the whip may be disqualified; the presiding officer decides; and in 2003 the 91st Amendment removes the split exception
visual.caption: The anti-defection law

slides.narration: The fifty second Amendment of nineteen eighty five added the Tenth Schedule. A member who leaves the party, or who disobeys the party whip without permission and is not forgiven, may be disqualified, and the presiding officer decides. The ninety first Amendment of two thousand three removed the exception for a split, leaving only a merger agreed by two thirds.

rows: Parliament meets for fewer days than in earlier decades
Committees study many bills and budgets in detail
Disruptions waste time and limit debate
Parliament still approves the budget and can remove a government
Bills may pass with limited discussion
Questions and debates keep ministers accountable

slides.narration: People hold different views. Some argue that Parliament meets for fewer days than in earlier decades, that disruptions waste time, and that bills may pass with limited discussion. Others argue that committees study many bills in detail, that Parliament still approves the budget and can remove a government, and that questions keep ministers accountable. Students should weigh the reasons.

Joint sitting (Article 108); Speaker presides; none for a money bill

slides.narration: To sum up. Bills may be government or private, ordinary or money. An ordinary bill passes three readings in each House and then gets assent. A joint sitting settles a deadlock on an ordinary bill, but not on a money bill. Parliament controls the executive by questions, the budget, committees and no confidence. The anti defection law dates from nineteen eighty five.

notes.title: Legislature: Notes

sections.heading: 1. Why a parliament, and why two Houses
sections.body_md:
A **legislature** is the organ of government that makes laws. In India it is **Parliament**. Its tasks are **law-making**, **representation** of the people and the States, **control of the executive** and **debate** on public issues.

India has a **bicameral** Parliament: the **Lok Sabha** speaks for the people and the **Rajya Sabha** for the States. A second House also allows **reconsideration** of a bill. Most States have a single House, the Legislative Assembly; only **six** have a Legislative Council (as of 2024).

key_terms.definition_md: The organ of government that makes laws and keeps watch over the executive.
Having two Houses in the legislature.
A system in which power is divided between a Union government and the governments of its units, the States.

rows: Debating and passing bills so that they become laws
Speaking for the people and for the States
Questioning ministers and being able to remove the government
A forum where public issues are discussed openly

visual.alt: Table of the four functions of Parliament: law-making; representation of the people and the States; control of the executive by questioning ministers and being able to remove the government; and debate on public issues

rows: One House for the people, one for the States
A bill is studied twice, which checks hasty decisions
The States are heard in making laws for the Union
Most States have one House; six have Legislative Councils (as of 2024)

visuals.alt: Table of reasons for two Houses: two kinds of representation, reconsideration of bills, federal balance, and in the States most have one House while six have a Legislative Council as of 2024

sections.heading: 2. The Rajya Sabha
sections.body_md:
The **Rajya Sabha** represents the **States**. It has at most **250** members: up to **238 elected** and **12 nominated** by the President for distinction in art, literature, science and social service. (As of 2024 the House has 245 members, of whom 233 are elected, with seats also for Delhi and Puducherry.)

The elected members are chosen **indirectly** by the elected members of the State Legislative Assemblies, by **proportional representation by the single transferable vote**. Seats are allotted broadly by **population**, so representation is **unequal**, unlike the US Senate.

The term is **six years**. The House is **permanent**: it is not dissolved, and about **one-third** of members retire every **second year**. The minimum age is **30**. The Vice-President is its ex officio Chairman.

key_terms.definition_md: The Council of States: the House of Parliament that represents the States and is a permanent House.
A system of proportional representation in which voters rank candidates and a candidate is elected on reaching a quota.
A member appointed by the President, not elected.
A House that is never dissolved as a whole, because its members retire in batches.

sections.heading: 3. The Lok Sabha and the powers of the Houses
sections.body_md:
The **Lok Sabha** represents the **people** and is **directly elected** by first past the post. The Constitution allows up to **550** elected members; there are **543** constituencies (as of 2024). The nomination of two Anglo-Indian members ended with the **104th Amendment** (passed 2019, in effect 2020). The term is **five years**, unless the House is **dissolved** earlier. The minimum age is **25**. The Speaker presides.

**Shared powers:** both Houses pass **ordinary bills** and **constitutional amendments**, and take part in electing the **President** and the **Vice-President**.

**Lok Sabha:** **money bills** start only here; the Rajya Sabha can only **delay a money bill for 14 days**; the **Speaker certifies** a money bill; only the Lok Sabha can pass a **no-confidence motion**; it votes on the **demands for grants**.

**Rajya Sabha:** under **Article 249**, a resolution by two-thirds of members present and voting lets Parliament make a law on a **State List** subject in the national interest; under **Article 312**, it can authorise a **new All India Service**.

The ending of the Lok Sabha before or at the end of its term, so that fresh elections are held.
A bill dealing only with matters such as taxes, borrowing and spending, introduced only in the Lok Sabha (Article 110).
A motion that, if passed by the Lok Sabha, shows the government has lost its support and must resign.

sections.heading: 4. How a bill becomes a law
sections.body_md:
A **government bill** is introduced by a **minister**; a **private member's bill** by a member who is not a minister, and it is rarely passed.

An **ordinary bill** goes through: **introduction and first reading**; **second reading**, with possible reference to a **committee**; **consideration** and voting, then the **third reading**; the **same stages in the other House**; and the **assent of the President**. The President may return an ordinary bill **once**; if it is passed again, assent must follow. A money bill cannot be returned.

If the Houses disagree on an ordinary bill, a **joint sitting** may be called (**Article 108**), presided over by the **Speaker**; the bill is decided by a majority of members present and voting. A **money bill** (**Article 110**) follows special rules and has **no joint sitting**.

key_terms.definition_md: A proposed law placed before the legislature.
A bill introduced by a member who is not a minister.
A meeting of both Houses together, called to settle a disagreement on an ordinary bill (Article 108).
The President's approval that turns a bill passed by Parliament into an Act.

sections.heading: 5. Control over the executive
sections.body_md:
In a parliamentary system the executive is **answerable** to the legislature. The instruments are:
- **Deliberation and discussion:** **Question Hour** (the first hour of a sitting), **Zero Hour** (a practice, not in the rules as such, for urgent matters without notice), **calling attention**, and the **adjournment motion**.
- **Approval or refusal** of laws.
- **Financial control:** the **budget** and **demands for grants** (voted only in the Lok Sabha); the **Comptroller and Auditor General** audits accounts and reports to Parliament; the **Public Accounts Committee** examines these reports.
- A **no-confidence motion** in the Lok Sabha.

The practice of raising urgent matters without prior notice, soon after Question Hour.
A motion to set aside the business of the day to discuss a definite matter of urgent public importance.
The authority that audits government accounts and reports to Parliament.

sections.heading: 6. Committees and Parliament regulating itself
sections.body_md:
**Standing committees** are permanent (for example the **Public Accounts Committee**) and include the **department-related standing committees**, begun in **1993**. **Joint parliamentary committees** are **ad hoc**, formed for a particular bill or matter, with members of both Houses. Committees matter because they study subjects **in detail**, hear **experts**, foster cooperation across parties and scrutinise the executive **through the year**.

The **Speaker** (Lok Sabha) and the **Chairman** (Rajya Sabha) **maintain order and discipline**. The **anti-defection law**: the **52nd Amendment (1985)** added the **Tenth Schedule**; a member who **leaves the party** or **disobeys its whip** without permission, and is not forgiven within fifteen days, can be **disqualified**; the **presiding officer decides**. The **91st Amendment (2003)** removed the **split** exception; a **merger** agreed by two-thirds is protected.

Some argue that the role of Parliament has **declined** (fewer sitting days, disruptions); others point to the work of **committees**.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Saying the Rajya Sabha is elected by all voters: it is chosen by the elected members of State Assemblies.
- Saying the Rajya Sabha can reject a money bill: it can only delay it for 14 days.
- Saying either House can pass a no-confidence motion: only the Lok Sabha.
- Using a joint sitting for a money bill: it is for ordinary bills only.
- Calling Zero Hour a rule of the Constitution: it is a practice.
- Crediting the 91st Amendment with starting the anti-defection law: the 52nd (1985) did.

**Tips:** state the date with any figure that can change ("as of 2024"); name the three readings in order; use some argue, others argue on the decline of Parliament; give an example from an imagined bill in longer answers.

questions.stem_md: Which pair of tasks forms the central work of a legislature such as the Parliament of India?

options.text_md: Carrying out laws and trying offenders
Making laws and keeping a watch on the executive
Collecting taxes and conducting elections
Appointing civil servants and commanding the armed forces

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Making laws and keeping a watch on the executive. A legislature frames laws and holds the government to account. Carrying out laws belongs to the executive, trying offenders to the courts, and elections are conducted by the Election Commission; appointing civil servants and commanding the forces are executive functions.

questions.stem_md: The imagined federation of Rhenia decides that its Union legislature will have two Houses. Which reason best fits the choice of two Houses for a federation?

options.text_md: Two Houses make every law pass twice as fast
A democracy is not allowed to have a single House
The second House exists only to elect the head of state
One House can speak for the people and the other for the units of the federation, and each can reconsider the work of the other

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** One House can speak for the people and the other for the units of the federation, and each can reconsider the work of the other. The usual argument for a second House is that it gives the units of a federation a voice and allows a bill to be reconsidered. Speed is not the aim, democracies do function with one House, and electing the head of state is only a small part of the task of a second House.

questions.stem_md: As of 2024, how many States of India have a Legislative Council as a second House of the State Legislature?

options.text_md: Six
Fourteen
Twenty
Not one

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Six. Only six States have a Legislative Council, and most States have a single House, the Legislative Assembly. The figures fourteen and twenty overstate the number, and zero is wrong since some Councils do exist.

questions.stem_md: Dr Anjali Mehra is elected to the Rajya Sabha from the imagined State of Palmora. Who voted in that election?

options.text_md: All the registered voters of Palmora
The Lok Sabha members elected from Palmora
The elected members of the Palmora Legislative Assembly
The Chief Minister and the ministers of Palmora alone

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The elected members of the Palmora Legislative Assembly. Rajya Sabha members are chosen indirectly by the elected members of the State Legislative Assembly. Ordinary voters elect the Assembly and the Lok Sabha, not the Rajya Sabha; Lok Sabha members and the ministers alone are not the electors.

questions.stem_md: The Constitution sets the maximum strength of the Rajya Sabha at 250 members. How many of them are nominated by the President, and for what reason?

options.text_md: Two, to represent a community
Twelve, to represent the Union Territories
Twelve, for distinction in art, literature, science and social service
Twenty-five, for service in the armed forces

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Twelve, for distinction in art, literature, science and social service. Twelve members are nominated for special knowledge or practical experience in art, literature, science and social service, and the other seats (238 at most) are elected. The remaining options give wrong numbers or invented purposes.

questions.stem_md: Radhika Nair is elected to the Rajya Sabha in 2026 and serves her full term without resigning. Her term ends in
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** 2032. The term is six years, so 2026 plus 6 gives 2032. Five years would give 2031, and 2028 is the sort of date that results from confusing the term with the two-yearly retirement of one-third of the House.

questions.stem_md: The Rajya Sabha is described as a permanent House because

options.text_md: its members are elected for life
it meets throughout the year without a break
its members cannot be removed by the Chairman
it is never dissolved as a whole, and about one-third of its members retire every two years

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** it is never dissolved as a whole, and about one-third of its members retire every two years. Continuity comes from the fact that the House is not dissolved and members retire in batches. Members serve for six years and not for life, sittings are held in sessions, and the Chairman's powers have nothing to do with the description.

questions.stem_md: In the third year after a general election, no leader can show majority support in the Lok Sabha, and the House is dissolved. What happens to the Rajya Sabha at that time?

options.text_md: It is dissolved at the same moment
It continues to exist, since it is not subject to dissolution
It is dissolved after six months
All its members retire together

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** It continues to exist, since it is not subject to dissolution. Only the Lok Sabha can be dissolved before its five years are over. The Rajya Sabha goes on, with its members retiring in batches, so the other options wrongly extend dissolution to it.

questions.stem_md: As of 2024, the Constitution allows the Lok Sabha up to 550 elected members, while the number of Lok Sabha constituencies is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** 543. There are 543 constituencies. The figure 550 is the constitutional maximum and not the actual number; 530 is the number the Constitution allows for the States, and 545 is not a figure the Constitution fixes for the Lok Sabha.

questions.stem_md: Which constitutional change ended the nomination of two Anglo-Indian members to the Lok Sabha?

options.text_md: The 42nd Amendment (1976)
The 104th Amendment (passed in 2019, in effect from 2020)
The 91st Amendment (2003)
The 52nd Amendment (1985)

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The 104th Amendment (passed in 2019, in effect from 2020). The 104th Amendment ended the nomination. The 42nd concerned wide changes of 1976, the 91st limited the size of the Council of Ministers, and the 52nd added the anti-defection provisions.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined federation of Rhenia, the second chamber gives every province exactly three seats, however large the province. In India, in contrast, Rajya Sabha seats are

options.text_md: equal for every State, exactly as in Rhenia
fixed each year by the Speaker according to the revenue of each State
allotted to the States broadly in proportion to population, so larger States have more seats
given only to the States that have a Legislative Council

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** allotted to the States broadly in proportion to population, so larger States have more seats. Representation in the Rajya Sabha is unequal and follows population broadly, which is a notable difference from systems like the American Senate or the imagined Rhenia. The Speaker has no role, and revenue or the presence of a Council does not decide the allotment.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Coastal Levy Bill proposes a new tax on exports of dried fish and is certified as a money bill. In which House can it be introduced?

options.text_md: Only in the Rajya Sabha
In either House, at the choice of the minister
In a joint sitting of both Houses
Only in the Lok Sabha

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Only in the Lok Sabha. A money bill is introduced only in the Lok Sabha. Ordinary bills can start in either House, and a joint sitting is a way of settling a disagreement, not a place where bills begin.

questions.stem_md: The Lok Sabha passes a money bill on 1 March and sends it to the Rajya Sabha, which takes no action. What is the position after 14 days?

options.text_md: The bill lapses and must be introduced afresh
A joint sitting must be called to decide it
The bill waits until the Rajya Sabha chooses to take it up
The bill is deemed passed by both Houses in the form the Lok Sabha passed it

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The bill is deemed passed by both Houses in the form the Lok Sabha passed it. The Rajya Sabha can only delay a money bill for 14 days, after which it is treated as passed. There is no lapse, no joint sitting for money bills, and no indefinite wait.

questions.stem_md: If a doubt arises whether the imagined Harbour Tax Bill is a money bill, whose certificate settles the question?

options.text_md: The Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
The Prime Minister
The Speaker of the Lok Sabha
The Chief Justice of India

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The Speaker of the Lok Sabha. The Speaker certifies a money bill, and that decision is final. The Chairman presides over the other House, and neither the Prime Minister nor the Chief Justice has this task.

questions.stem_md: Members of the Opposition in the Rajya Sabha wish to pass a no-confidence motion to remove the Council of Ministers. Why will this not succeed?

options.text_md: The Rajya Sabha is not allowed to discuss the Council of Ministers
Only the Lok Sabha can pass a no-confidence motion that forces the Council to resign
A no-confidence motion can be passed only by the President
The Council is answerable to the Vice-President

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Only the Lok Sabha can pass a no-confidence motion that forces the Council to resign. The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha alone, so only that House can pass the motion. The Rajya Sabha can discuss and criticise ministers, the President does not pass motions, and the Vice-President is not the authority to whom the Council answers.

questions.stem_md: Parliament wishes to make a law on a subject on the State List because it has become a national concern. Under Article 249, which step must come first?

options.text_md: The Rajya Sabha passes a resolution, supported by two-thirds of the members present and voting, that this is necessary in the national interest
The Lok Sabha passes a resolution by a simple majority
Every State Legislature passes its own resolution
The President issues an ordinance on the subject

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The Rajya Sabha passes a resolution, supported by two-thirds of the members present and voting, that this is necessary in the national interest. Article 249 gives the initiative to the Rajya Sabha, which speaks for the States, and requires a two-thirds majority present and voting. A Lok Sabha resolution, state resolutions and an ordinance are not the route this Article provides.

questions.stem_md: The creation of a new All India Service requires a resolution of

options.text_md: the Lok Sabha, by a simple majority
the Rajya Sabha, supported by two-thirds of its members present and voting
the State Legislative Councils
the Union Public Service Commission

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** the Rajya Sabha, supported by two-thirds of its members present and voting. Under Article 312 the Rajya Sabha must pass the resolution by two-thirds of those present and voting. The Lok Sabha has no such special role here, Councils exist in few States, and the Commission recruits for existing services.

questions.stem_md: A minister rises in the Lok Sabha, introduces the imagined Village Libraries Bill and states its aim; members do not yet discuss the clauses. This stage is

options.text_md: the second reading
the third reading
the assent
the introduction and first reading

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** the introduction and first reading. At the first reading the bill is only introduced. The second reading is when the principles and clauses are debated, the third reading is the final vote, and assent comes from the President at the end.

questions.stem_md: During the second reading of the imagined Urban Lakes Protection Bill, members feel that its clauses need a closer study with expert opinion. What is the usual step?

options.text_md: The bill is referred to a committee, which studies it and reports back to the House
The bill is sent to the President for advice
The bill is dropped without a vote
The bill passes to the other House without any vote

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The bill is referred to a committee, which studies it and reports back to the House. A bill may be referred to a committee after the second reading for detailed study. The President does not advise at this stage, dropping a bill is not what a closer study means, and a bill must be voted on before moving to the other House.

questions.stem_md: Both Houses have passed an ordinary bill. The President returns it with a message asking Parliament to reconsider it, and Parliament passes it again, with or without changes. What follows?

options.text_md: The bill lapses
The bill must go to a joint sitting
The President cannot withhold assent to it
The President may return it again, with no limit

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The President cannot withhold assent to it. An ordinary bill can be returned once; if Parliament passes it again, assent must be given. There is no lapse, a joint sitting is for disagreement between the Houses, and a second return is not allowed.

questions.stem_md: A joint sitting of the two Houses to settle a disagreement over an ordinary bill is presided over by the

options.text_md: Vice-President
Prime Minister
Speaker of the Lok Sabha
President

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Speaker of the Lok Sabha. The Speaker presides at a joint sitting. The Vice-President chairs only the Rajya Sabha, the Prime Minister is a member of one House, and the President summons the sitting but does not preside.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined case of the Coastal Fisheries Bill, an ordinary bill, the Lok Sabha passes it and the Rajya Sabha rejects it. Which statement is correct?

options.text_md: A joint sitting may be called under Article 108, and the bill is decided by a majority of members present and voting
The bill is dead and can never be tried again
The Lok Sabha decides alone, as with a money bill
The President decides which House is right

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A joint sitting may be called under Article 108, and the bill is decided by a majority of members present and voting. For an ordinary bill, disagreement between the Houses can be settled at a joint sitting. The bill is not dead, the Lok Sabha does not decide alone since this is not a money bill, and the President does not rule between the Houses.

questions.stem_md: The Rajya Sabha returns the imagined Harbour Tax Bill, certified as a money bill, with several suggestions, and the Lok Sabha rejects all of them. What happens next?

options.text_md: A joint sitting under Article 108 is called
The bill is withdrawn
The Rajya Sabha is asked to vote again until it agrees
The bill goes forward in the form the Lok Sabha passed it, since a money bill has no joint sitting

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The bill goes forward in the form the Lok Sabha passed it, since a money bill has no joint sitting. The Lok Sabha view prevails on a money bill, and Article 108 does not apply to it. The bill is not withdrawn, and the Rajya Sabha has no power to hold it back by repeated voting.

questions.stem_md: Meenal Rao, who is not a minister, introduces a bill in the Lok Sabha on a right to rest for night-shift workers in the imagined session. This is a

options.text_md: government bill
private member's bill
money bill
budget bill

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** private member's bill. A bill introduced by a member who is not a minister is a private member's bill. A government bill is introduced by a minister, and a money bill and a budget bill concern taxation and spending and are brought on behalf of the government.

questions.stem_md: In the first hour of a sitting, a member asks the imagined Minister of Fisheries a question about the number of cold-storage units built under a scheme, and the minister replies. This part of the day is called

options.text_md: Question Hour
Zero Hour
the adjournment motion
the third reading

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Question Hour. Questions to ministers in the first hour make up Question Hour. Zero Hour follows it and has no notice, the adjournment motion sets aside the business of the day, and the third reading is a stage of a bill.

questions.stem_md: Just after Question Hour, Prakash Iyer stands and raises, without earlier notice, the matter of a school bus accident in his constituency. The practice by which such matters are raised is called

options.text_md: a no-confidence motion
Zero Hour
a money bill
a joint sitting

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Zero Hour. Raising urgent matters soon after Question Hour is Zero Hour, a practice and not a rule written in the formal rules of procedure. The other options are a motion to remove the government, a kind of bill, and a meeting of both Houses.

questions.stem_md: Members give notice of a motion that, if admitted, would set aside the business of the day to discuss a recent factory fire, a definite matter of urgent public importance. Which instrument are they using?

options.text_md: A no-confidence motion
Zero Hour
An adjournment motion
A private member's bill

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** An adjournment motion. An adjournment motion draws attention to a definite urgent matter and interrupts the normal business. A no-confidence motion tests the government's majority, Zero Hour sets aside no business, and a private member's bill proposes a law.

questions.stem_md: A report of the Comptroller and Auditor General says that an imagined ministry spent 40 crore rupees on projects without Parliament's sanction. Which parliamentary committee will examine the report?

options.text_md: The Business Advisory Committee
The Committee on Privileges
A select committee on a bill
The Public Accounts Committee

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The Public Accounts Committee. Audit reports on government spending go to the Public Accounts Committee. The Business Advisory Committee arranges time for business, the Committee on Privileges deals with the rights of members, and a select committee studies a particular bill.

questions.stem_md: The Comptroller and Auditor General

options.text_md: prepares the annual budget
recruits civil servants for the Union
settles disputes between States
audits government accounts and submits reports that are placed before Parliament

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** audits government accounts and submits reports that are placed before Parliament. The office audits the accounts of the Union and the States and reports to Parliament through the President. The budget is prepared by the executive, recruitment is by the Commissions, and disputes between States are dealt with by other bodies.

questions.stem_md: One reason why department-related standing committees are valued is that

options.text_md: they pass laws on behalf of Parliament
they replace Question Hour
they study the work and budgets of ministries in detail through the year, away from the heat of floor debates
they elect the Speaker

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** they study the work and budgets of ministries in detail through the year, away from the heat of floor debates. Committees allow close, continuous scrutiny in a smaller setting. They recommend and report but do not pass laws, Question Hour continues alongside them, and the Speaker is elected by the Lok Sabha.

questions.stem_md: Members of both Houses are chosen for a panel to examine the imagined Urban Lakes Protection Bill, and the panel is to end its life once it reports. Such a body is best described as

options.text_md: a permanent committee of the Lok Sabha alone
an ad hoc committee with members from both Houses, set up for a particular bill or matter
a committee of the President and the Prime Minister
the committee that fixes the sitting days of Parliament

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** an ad hoc committee with members from both Houses, set up for a particular bill or matter. A joint committee has members of both Houses and is formed for a particular purpose, after which it ends. It is not permanent or confined to one House, and it does not include the President and Prime Minister or fix sitting dates.

questions.stem_md: Karan Sethi, a Lok Sabha member of the imagined Unity Party, votes against the Village Libraries Bill although his party issued a whip to vote for it. He had no permission, and his party did not condone the act within fifteen days. Who decides whether he is disqualified under the Tenth Schedule?

options.text_md: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha
The Election Commission
The Prime Minister
The Chairman of the Rajya Sabha

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The Speaker of the Lok Sabha. The presiding officer of the House to which the member belongs decides, so the Speaker decides for a Lok Sabha member. The Election Commission, the Prime Minister and the other House's Chairman have no such task.

questions.stem_md: Before 2003, a group of one-third of a party's legislators could leave the party without being disqualified. This exception for a split was removed by the

options.text_md: 52nd Amendment (1985)
91st Amendment (2003)
44th Amendment (1978)
104th Amendment (2019)

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** 91st Amendment (2003). The 91st Amendment removed the split exception. The 52nd Amendment first introduced the anti-defection law (with that exception), the 44th concerned advice to the President, and the 104th ended the nomination of Anglo-Indian members.

questions.stem_md: The Tenth Schedule, which provides for disqualification on the ground of defection, was added by the

options.text_md: 42nd Amendment (1976)
91st Amendment (2003)
44th Amendment (1978)
52nd Amendment (1985)

questions.stem_md: In an imagined newspaper debate, one writer says Parliament matters less than before because it meets for fewer days each year. Another replies that committees now study many bills in detail. Which statement best describes the two positions?

The first claim is plainly right and the second plainly wrong
The second claim is plainly right and the first plainly wrong

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Each points to a different kind of evidence, so a fair judgment weighs sitting time and committee scrutiny together. Choose the correct option.

questions.stem_md: State any two functions of the Parliament of India.
questions.solution_md: Two functions with a brief explanation.

answer.model_answer_md: Parliament **makes laws** for the country and **controls the executive** through questions, debates and the power to remove a government that loses the Lok Sabha's support. It also **represents** the people and the States, and provides a forum for **debate** on public matters.

marking_scheme.step: Control of the executive, representation or debate, explained

questions.stem_md: Why does India have a Parliament of two Houses?
questions.solution_md: Representation of the States as well as the people, and reconsideration.

answer.model_answer_md: India is a **federation** with many States and a very large population, so one House, the **Lok Sabha**, represents the people directly, while the **Rajya Sabha** represents the States. A second House also lets a bill be **reconsidered**, which checks hasty decisions.

marking_scheme.step: A House for the people and a House for the States

questions.stem_md: How are the elected members of the Rajya Sabha chosen?
questions.solution_md: Indirect election by the Assembly members, with the method of voting.

answer.model_answer_md: They are chosen **indirectly**: the **elected members of the State Legislative Assembly** of each State vote, using **proportional representation by the single transferable vote**. Voters at large do not elect them, since the House is meant to represent the States.

marking_scheme.step: Elected by the elected members of the State Legislative Assembly
Proportional representation by single transferable vote

questions.stem_md: State two differences between the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha in the term of members and in the way the House continues.
questions.solution_md: The term of members and the continuity of each House.

answer.model_answer_md: Lok Sabha members serve for **five years**, unless the House is **dissolved earlier**. Rajya Sabha members serve for **six years**, and the House is **never dissolved**: about **one-third** of its members retire every second year and new members take their place.

marking_scheme.step: Lok Sabha: five years; can be dissolved
Rajya Sabha: six years; permanent House with one-third retiring every two years

questions.stem_md: What can the Rajya Sabha do about a money bill that the Lok Sabha has passed?
questions.solution_md: Only a delay of 14 days, with the Lok Sabha having the final say.

answer.model_answer_md: It cannot reject or change the bill. It may only **return it with recommendations** within **14 days**. If it does nothing in that time, the bill is **deemed passed**, and the **Lok Sabha** may accept or reject the recommendations.

marking_scheme.step: Can only return it with recommendations within 14 days
Deemed passed after 14 days; the Lok Sabha decides on the recommendations

questions.stem_md: State the special powers that the Rajya Sabha has under Article 249 and Article 312.
questions.solution_md: The two special powers and the majority required.

answer.model_answer_md: Under **Article 249**, a resolution of the Rajya Sabha supported by **two-thirds** of members present and voting lets Parliament make a law on a **State List** subject in the **national interest**. Under **Article 312**, a similar resolution lets Parliament create a **new All India Service**.

marking_scheme.step: Article 249: law on a State List subject in the national interest
Article 312: a new All India Service, by a two-thirds resolution

questions.stem_md: Distinguish Question Hour from Zero Hour.
questions.solution_md: Question Hour is formal and noticed; Zero Hour is a practice.

answer.model_answer_md: **Question Hour** is the first hour of a sitting in which members put questions to ministers, usually with prior notice, and ministers answer. **Zero Hour** follows it and is a **practice**, not part of the formal rules as such, in which members raise urgent matters without prior notice.

marking_scheme.step: Question Hour: questions to ministers in the first hour
Zero Hour: a practice of raising urgent matters without notice

questions.stem_md: How do the Comptroller and Auditor General and the Public Accounts Committee help Parliament control government spending?
questions.solution_md: The auditor reports and the committee examines.

answer.model_answer_md: The **Comptroller and Auditor General** audits government accounts and reports to **Parliament**. The **Public Accounts Committee** then examines these reports and questions officials, to check whether money was spent as **Parliament approved**, and reports its findings to the House.

marking_scheme.step: The auditor audits the accounts and reports to Parliament
The Public Accounts Committee examines the reports to check spending as approved

questions.stem_md: Distinguish a government bill from a private member's bill.
questions.solution_md: Who introduces the bill and the chance of passing.

answer.model_answer_md: A **government bill** is introduced by a **minister** and carries the government's policy, so it usually has the time and the support to pass. A **private member's bill** is introduced by a member who is **not a minister**, in the limited time set aside for such members, and is rarely passed.

marking_scheme.step: Government bill: introduced by a minister, carries policy
Private member's bill: introduced by a non-minister, rarely passed

questions.stem_md: What did the 91st Amendment (2003) change in the anti-defection law?
questions.solution_md: The split exception was removed; only a merger of two-thirds remains.

answer.model_answer_md: It **removed the exception for a split**, under which a group of one-third of a party's legislators could leave without disqualification. After it, only a **merger** agreed by **two-thirds** of the party's legislators is protected, which makes it harder for small groups to change sides.

marking_scheme.step: Removed the exception for a split of one-third
Only a merger agreed by two-thirds is protected

questions.stem_md: Describe three special powers of the Lok Sabha.
questions.solution_md: Three special powers of the Lok Sabha.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Money bills** can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha.
2. The **Rajya Sabha** can only delay a money bill for 14 days, and the **Speaker** certifies whether a bill is a money bill.
3. Only the Lok Sabha can pass a **no-confidence motion**, which forces the Council of Ministers to resign; it also votes on the demands for grants.

marking_scheme.step: Money bills start only in the Lok Sabha
Rajya Sabha can only delay for 14 days; the Speaker certifies
Only the Lok Sabha passes a no-confidence motion

questions.stem_md: Describe three special features or powers of the Rajya Sabha.
questions.solution_md: Representation of the States and the two special powers.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. It represents the **States** in Parliament, and its members are elected by the elected members of the State Legislative Assemblies.
2. Under **Article 249**, it can authorise Parliament to make a law on a State List subject in the national interest.
3. Under **Article 312**, it can authorise the creation of a **new All India Service**.

questions.stem_md: Describe the stages through which an ordinary bill passes in the House where it is first introduced.
questions.solution_md: Three stages in order.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Introduction and first reading:** the bill is introduced and its purpose stated.
2. **Second reading:** the principles and clauses are discussed, and the bill may be referred to a **committee**.
3. **Consideration and third reading:** the clauses are voted on and amended if needed, and the final vote is taken.

marking_scheme.step: Second reading, with possible committee reference

questions.stem_md: Explain when a joint sitting of Parliament is held and how it decides an ordinary bill.
questions.solution_md: The occasion, the presiding officer and the decision.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. If the two Houses **disagree** on an ordinary bill, for example when one rejects it, a joint sitting may be called under **Article 108**.
2. The **Speaker** presides.
3. The bill is decided by a **majority of the members present and voting**; as the Lok Sabha is larger, its view is likely to prevail. A money bill has no joint sitting.

marking_scheme.step: Disagreement on an ordinary bill: Article 108
Majority of members present and voting

questions.stem_md: Name the two kinds of parliamentary committees and explain why committees matter.
questions.solution_md: The two kinds and their importance.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Standing committees**, including the **department-related standing committees**, are permanent and examine ministries, budgets and bills.
2. **Joint parliamentary committees** are **ad hoc**, formed for a particular bill or matter, with members from both Houses.
3. Committees matter because they study subjects **in detail**, hear **experts** and save the time of the House.

questions.stem_md: Explain the anti-defection law and the two amendments connected with it.
questions.solution_md: The Tenth Schedule, the presiding officer and the 2003 change.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The **52nd Amendment (1985)** added the **Tenth Schedule**, which provides for disqualification of a member who **leaves the party** or **disobeys its whip** without permission.
2. The **Speaker** or the **Chairman** decides the question.
3. The **91st Amendment (2003)** removed the **split** exception, leaving only mergers.

questions.stem_md: Describe any three ways in which Parliament controls the executive.
questions.solution_md: Three instruments of control.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Through **Question Hour**, Zero Hour and debates, members hold ministers to account.
2. Through **financial control**: money cannot be spent without Parliament's approval of the budget, and the **Public Accounts Committee** reviews spending.
3. Through a **no-confidence motion**, the Lok Sabha can force the Council of Ministers to resign.

questions.stem_md: Compare the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha in respect of representation, strength, election, term and minimum age.
questions.solution_md: Five points of comparison.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The **Lok Sabha** represents the **people**, and the **Rajya Sabha** the **States**.
2. The Constitution allows the Lok Sabha up to 550 elected members, with 543 constituencies (as of 2024); the Rajya Sabha has at most 250, of whom 12 are nominated.
3. Lok Sabha members are **directly elected** by first past the post; Rajya Sabha members are **indirectly elected** by single transferable vote.
4. The Lok Sabha serves **five years** and can be dissolved; the Rajya Sabha is **permanent**, with six-year terms.
5. The minimum age is **25** and **30** respectively.

questions.stem_md: Explain the powers that both Houses share and the special powers of each House.
questions.solution_md: Shared powers, then the Lok Sabha's and the Rajya Sabha's special powers.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Both Houses pass **ordinary bills** and **constitutional amendments**, and take part in electing the **President** and the **Vice-President**.
2. **Money bills** start only in the Lok Sabha, and the Rajya Sabha can only delay them for **14 days**.
3. The **Speaker** certifies a money bill, and only the Lok Sabha can pass a **no-confidence motion**.
4. The Rajya Sabha can authorise a law on a **State List** subject in the national interest (**Article 249**).
5. It can also authorise a new **All India Service** (**Article 312**).

questions.stem_md: Explain, step by step, how the imagined Village Libraries Bill, an ordinary bill introduced in the Lok Sabha, becomes a law.
questions.solution_md: Five steps from introduction to assent.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. A minister **introduces** the bill and states its aim (**first reading**).
2. At the **second reading** its principles and clauses are debated, and it may be sent to a **committee**.
3. The House votes on the clauses and the bill at the **third reading**.
4. The **Rajya Sabha** takes it through the same stages; if the Houses disagree, a **joint sitting** under Article 108 may be called.
5. The **President's assent** makes it an Act.

marking_scheme.step: Other House; joint sitting on disagreement

questions.stem_md: Explain the instruments through which Parliament controls the executive.
questions.solution_md: Discussion, laws, finance, committees and the no-confidence motion.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Deliberation and discussion** include Question Hour, Zero Hour, calling attention and the adjournment motion.
2. Parliament can **approve or refuse laws** proposed by the government.
3. **Financial control** works through the budget and the demands for grants.
4. The **Public Accounts Committee** examines spending, using the reports of the **Comptroller and Auditor General**.
5. A **no-confidence motion** can remove the Council of Ministers, and committees study the work of ministries.

marking_scheme.step: Deliberation: Question Hour, Zero Hour and others
Public Accounts Committee and the auditor

questions.stem_md: Describe the kinds of parliamentary committees and explain why they are important.
questions.solution_md: Two kinds, and reasons of detail, experts and continuous scrutiny.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Standing committees** are permanent; they include the Public Accounts Committee and the **department-related standing committees**, begun in 1993.
2. **Joint parliamentary committees** are **ad hoc** bodies of members of both Houses for a particular bill or matter.
3. Committees study subjects **in detail**, which the full House has no time to do.
4. They hear **experts** and the public.
5. Members of different parties often work more closely there, and the executive is scrutinised through the year.

questions.stem_md: Some argue that the role of Parliament has declined, while others point to the work of its committees. Examine both views.
questions.solution_md: Both views with reasons, and a balanced conclusion.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Some argue that Parliament now meets for **fewer days** than in earlier decades.
2. They add that **disruptions** waste time, and bills may be passed with limited debate.
3. Others point to the **committees**, where bills and budgets are studied in detail.
4. They also note that Parliament still **approves the budget**, questions ministers and can remove a government.
5. A balanced view weighs both with data on sitting days, debate and committee work.

marking_scheme.step: Continuing powers over the budget and the executive
